claim: Cannabis is the most commonly consumed illicit drug around the world with 181.8 million estimated regular users aged 15-64.
source: With 181.8 million estimated regular users aged 15 – 64, cannabis is the most commonly consumed illicit drug around the world (UNODC, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to UNODC, 2015

claim: 7.5% of pregnant women between 18 and 25 years of age in the U.S. use cannabis.
source: In fact, data collected from 2002 to 2014 in the U.S. indicates that 7.5% of pregnant women between 18 and 25 years of age use cannabis, while the rate of use in all pregnant women is approximately 4% (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2017

claim: The rate of cannabis use in all pregnant women in the U.S. is approximately 4%.
source: In fact, data collected from 2002 to 2014 in the U.S. indicates that 7.5% of pregnant women between 18 and 25 years of age use cannabis, while the rate of use in all pregnant women is approximately 4% (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2017

claim: 48% of women who used cannabis in the year prior to their pregnancy continued to smoke cannabis throughout pregnancy.
source: A longitudinal prospective study on drug use in pregnancy showed that 48% of women who used cannabis in the year prior to their pregnancy continued to smoke cannabis throughout pregnancy (Moore et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2010

claim: 70% of pregnant and non-pregnant women believe that there is little or no harm in using cannabis once or twice per week.
source: Moreover, 70% of pregnant and non-pregnant women believe that there is little or no harm in using cannabis once or twice per week (Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ko et al., 2015

claim: Epidemiological studies of children with a history of in utero cannabis exposure reveal normal intelligence scores but altered cognition and executive functions.
source: Epidemiological studies of children with a history of in utero cannabis exposure reveal normal intelligence scores but altered cognition and executive functions (attention, memory, concentration, inhibitory control) and higher levels of depression and anxiety during adolescence (Grant et al., 2018; Higuera-Matas et al., 2015) have been reported.
evidence: Supported by citations to Grant et al., 2018 and Higuera-Matas et al., 2015

claim: Children with a history of in utero cannabis exposure have higher levels of depression and anxiety during adolescence.
source: Epidemiological studies of children with a history of in utero cannabis exposure reveal normal intelligence scores but altered cognition and executive functions (attention, memory, concentration, inhibitory control) and higher levels of depression and anxiety during adolescence (Grant et al., 2018; Higuera-Matas et al., 2015) have been reported.
evidence: Supported by citations to Grant et al., 2018 and Higuera-Matas et al., 2015

claim: Prenatal exposure to cannabinoids has been linked to alterations in locomotor, learning, memory, emotional functions and social interaction in animal studies.
source: In animal studies, prenatal exposure to various regimens of cannabinoids has been linked to alterations in locomotor, learning, memory, emotional functions and social interaction (Campolongo et al., 2011; Higuera-Matas et al., 2015; Vargish et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campolongo et al., 2011; Higuera-Matas et al., 2015; Vargish et al., 2017

claim: Most animal studies investigating prenatal cannabinoid exposure effects used male progeny only.
source: A major caveat is that most studies investigated effects using male progeny only.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of previous research

claim: Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) efficiently crosses the placental barrier and reaches the fetus.
source: Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the major psychoactive ingredient in marijuana and other cannabis-based preparations, efficiently crosses the placental barrier and reaches the fetus (Hurd et al., 2005; Hutchings et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurd et al., 2005 and Hutchings et al., 1989

claim: CB1R is the main target of THC in the brain.
source: In the brain, cannabinoid receptor type 1 (CB1R) is the main target of THC.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about THC mechanism

claim: The endocannabinoid system through CB1R has been implicated in neuronal proliferation, migration, morphogenesis and synaptogenesis.
source: The endocannabinoid system, mainly through CB1R, has been implicated in neuronal proliferation, migration, morphogenesis and synaptogenesis (Berghuis et al., 2007; Harkany et al., 2007; Maccarrone et al., 2014; Mulder et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berghuis et al., 2007; Harkany et al., 2007; Maccarrone et al., 2014; Mulder et al., 2008

claim: Prenatal treatment with vehicle solution in control dams (SHAM group) did not alter sociability in adult rats of either sex.
source: Prenatal treatment from GD 5 to GD 20 with vehicle solution in control dams (SHAM group) did not alter sociability (social interaction), anxiety (elevated plus maze), and cognition (temporal order and object recognition memory tasks) in adult rats of either sex.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 showing no significant differences between SHAM and Naive animals

claim: Prenatal cannabinoid exposure (PCE) reduced social interaction in adult male rats.
source: We found that PCE impaired specific components of social interactions in adult male rats. Thus, PCE males had less contact and spent less time interacting with their congeners than those exposed in-utero to vehicle (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B

claim: Adult male progeny from dams exposed during gestation to WIN had less contact with their congeners than SHAM-animals.
source: Adult male progeny from dams exposed during gestation to WIN had less contact (A): F(sex x treat)1,28=15.54, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA) and spent less time interacting with their congeners than SHAM-animals (B): F(sex x treat)1,28=7.09, p<0.05, two-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1

claim: The social behavior of female littermates was normal after prenatal cannabinoid exposure.
source: In contrast, the social behavior of female littermates was normal.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1

claim: Sniffing behaviors were impaired in PCE males.
source: Detailed exploration of the various parameters of social interaction revealed that sniffing (Figure 1C–D) and playing (Figure 1E) behaviors were impaired in PCE males while the number of attacks remained unchanged (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: Playing behaviors were impaired in PCE males.
source: Detailed exploration of the various parameters of social interaction revealed that sniffing (Figure 1C–D) and playing (Figure 1E) behaviors were impaired in PCE males while the number of attacks remained unchanged (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The number of attacks remained unchanged in PCE males.
source: Detailed exploration of the various parameters of social interaction revealed that sniffing (Figure 1C–D) and playing (Figure 1E) behaviors were impaired in PCE males while the number of attacks remained unchanged (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The low socialization in PCE males was unlikely due to impaired motor locomotion.
source: The low socialization in PCE males was unlikely due to impaired motor locomotion, as we found no significant change in the distance traveled between WIN and SHAM groups during testing (3758 ± 117.8 cm, n = 10; and 3779 ± 228.8 cm, n = 8; t(7) = 0.02, p>0.05, t-test; SHAM- and WIN-exposed rats, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in distance traveled

claim: No differences between WIN- and SHAM prenatally-exposed rats were found in the elevated plus maze test.
source: No differences between WIN- and SHAM prenatally-exposed rats were found in the elevated plus maze. Specifically, there was no change in the percentage of time spent in the open arms (Figure 2A), percentage of open arm entries (Figure 2B), in the time spent in the open and close arms (Figure 2C–D), number of closed-arm entries ([F(treat x sex)1,29 = 0.195 p=0.662]; data not shown), stretch-attended posture ([F(treat x sex)1,29 = 0.167 p=0.685]; data not shown) and frequency of head-dippings ([F(treat x sex)1,29 = 0.338 p=0.565; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A-D and statistical analyses

claim: Adult SHAM and WIN-exposed animals of both sexes displayed identical discrimination index and exploration time in the temporal order memory task.
source: Regarding their cognitive abilities, adult SHAM and WIN-exposed animals of both sexes displayed identical discrimination index and exploration time in both the temporal order memory task (Figure 2E–F) and the novel object recognition test (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E-F

claim: Adult SHAM and WIN-exposed animals of both sexes displayed identical discrimination index and exploration time in the novel object recognition test.
source: Regarding their cognitive abilities, adult SHAM and WIN-exposed animals of both sexes displayed identical discrimination index and exploration time in both the temporal order memory task (Figure 2E–F) and the novel object recognition test (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2G-H

claim: Social interaction was specifically impaired in PCE males while locomotion, anxiety and cognition were spared in both sexes.
source: Thus, while social interaction was specifically impaired in PCE males, locomotion, anxiety and cognition were spared in both sexes.
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings from Figures 1 and 2

claim: eCB-LTD in the accumbens is not affected by PCE.
source: The data indicated that eCB-LTD in the accumbens is not affected by PCE (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: Low-frequency stimulation induces LTD at accumbens synapses in both SHAM- and WIN-exposed male rats.
source: Average time-courses of mean fEPSPs showing that low-frequency stimulation (indicated by arrow) induces LTD at accumbens synapses in both SHAM- (white circles, n = 5) and WIN- (green circles, n = 5) exposed male rats.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: PCE does not affect eCB-LTD in male accumbens.
source: Individual experiments (grey) and group average (tan), before (baseline) and after (40 min) LTD induction showing that PCE does not affect eCB-LTD in male accumbens. In SHAM male rats: 2.518 ± 0.145 mV.ms before LTD versus 1.872 ± 0.124 mV.ms after LTD induction (n = 5, p<0.05, paired t-test). In WIN male: 2.152 ± 0.224 mV.ms before LTD versus 1.696 ± 0.073 mV.ms after LTD induction (n = 5, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Prenatal WIN exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group in the accumbens.
source: Individual experiments (grey) and group average (white represents SHAM; orange represents WIN), before (baseline) and after (40 min) LTD induction showing that prenatal WIN exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group. In SHAM female: 2.350 ± 0.191 mV.ms before LTD versus 1.800 ± 0.182 mV.ms after LTD induction (n = 6, p<0.05, paired t-test). In WIN female: 2.461 ± 0.439 mV.ms before LTD versus 1.833 ± 0.381 mV.ms after LTD induction (n = 4, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Tetanic stimulation induced a robust eCB-LTD of excitatory synapses onto layer 5 mPFC pyramidal neurons in mPFC slices prepared from adult SHAM male and female rats.
source: We first established that tetanic stimulation induced a robust eCB-LTD of excitatory synapses onto layer 5 mPFC pyramidal neurons in mPFC slices prepared from adult SHAM male and female rats (Figure 4A–B–C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A-D

claim: eCB-LTD in the mPFC was absent in WIN-exposed males.
source: In marked contrast to the accumbens, eCB-LTD in the mPFC was absent in WIN-exposed males (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B

claim: LTD was normal in PCE female littermates in the mPFC.
source: Strikingly, LTD was normal in PCE female littermates (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D

claim: Low-frequency stimulation (10 min at 10 Hz) induced LTD of evoked fEPSPs recorded in the mPFC in SHAM but not in WIN prenatally-exposed male rats.
source: Average time-courses of mea field EPSPs showing that low-frequency stimulation (10 min at 10 Hz, arrow) induced LTD of evoked fEPSPs recorded in the mPFC in SHAM (n = 7; white circles), but not in WIN (n = 17; green circles) prenatally-exposed male rats.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In SHAM male rats, fEPSP amplitude decreased from 0.185 ± 0.006 mV before LTD to 0.150 ± 0.007 mV after LTD induction (n = 7, p<0.05).
source: In SHAM rats: 0.185 ± 0.006 mV before LTD versus 0.150 ± 0.007 mV after LTD induction (n = 7, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In WIN-exposed male animals, fEPSP amplitude did not significantly change from 0.197 ± 0.008 mV before LTD to 0.189 ± 0.009 mV after LTD induction (n = 17, p>0.05).
source: In WIN animals: 0.197 ± 0.008 mV before LTD versus 0.189 ± 0.009 mV after LTD induction (n = 17, p>0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Prenatal WIN exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group in the mPFC.
source: Individual experiments (grey) and group average (white represents SHAM; orange represents WIN), before (baseline) and after (40 min) LTD induction showing that prenatal WIN exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group. In SHAM female rats: 0.204 ± 0.009 mV before LTD versus 0.168 ± 0.010 mV after LTD induction (n = 5, p<0.05, paired t-test). In WIN female rats: 0.255 ± 0.012 mV before LTD versus 0.214 ± 0.013 mV after LTD induction (n = 13, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4D

claim: A similar sex-specific ablation of eCB-LTD in the progeny of dams exposed to THC was observed.
source: In a second series of experiments a similar sex-specific ablation of eCB-LTD in the progeny of dams exposed to THC, the main psychoactive component of cannabis, was observed (5 mg/kg, s.c. GD5-20; Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5

claim: Low-frequency stimulation (10 min at 10 Hz) induced LTD of evoked fEPSPs recorded in the mPFC in SHAM but not in THC prenatally-exposed male rats.
source: Average time-courses of men field EPSPs showing that low-frequency stimulation (10 min at 10 Hz, arrow) induced LTD of evoked fEPSPs recorded in the mPFC in SHAM (n = 4; white circles), but not in THC (n = 6; green circles) prenatally-exposed male rats.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A

claim: In SHAM male rats exposed to THC vehicle, fEPSP amplitude decreased from 0.239 ± 0.030 mV before LTD to 0.202 ± 0.028 mV after LTD induction (n = 4, p<0.05).
source: In SHAM rats: 0.239 ± 0.030 mV before LTD versus 0.202 ± 0.028 mV after LTD induction (n = 4, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In THC-exposed male animals, fEPSP amplitude did not significantly change from 0.244 ± 0.023 mV before LTD to 0.236 ± 0.019 mV after LTD induction (n = 6, p>0.05).
source: In THC animals: 0.244 ± 0.023 mV before LTD versus 0.236 ± 0.019 mV after LTD induction (n = 6, p>0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Prenatal THC exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group in the mPFC.
source: Individual experiments (grey) and group average (white represents SHAM; orange represents THC), before (baseline) and after (40 min) LTD induction showing that prenatal THC exposure does not alter LTD in the female exposed group. In SHAM female rats: 0.211 ± 0.011 mV before LTD versus 0.183 ± 0.010 mV after LTD induction (n = 6, p<0.05, paired t-test). In THC female rats: 0.234 ± 0.030 mV before LTD versus 0.177 ± 0.030 mV after LTD induction (n = 4, p<0.05, paired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5D

claim: mGlu2/3-mediated LTD was indistinguishable in SHAM- and WIN-exposed male and female.
source: In contrast to the lack of eCB-LTD, mGlu2/3-mediated LTD was indistinguishable in SHAM- and WIN-exposed male and female (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 A-B ).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 A-B

claim: Theta-burst stimulation (TBS) induces similar levels of NMDAR-dependent LTP at mPFC pyramidal synapses independent of sex and prenatal treatment.
source: Similarly, theta-burst stimulation (TBS) induces similar levels of NMDAR-dependent LTP at mPFC pyramidal synapses independent of sex and prenatal treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 C-D-E-F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 C-D-E-F

claim: Prenatal THC does not affect prefrontal LTP at adulthood.
source: We also confirmed that prenatal THC does not affect prefrontal LTP at adulthood (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: mPFC neurons in WIN-exposed rats showed impaired membrane reaction profiles in response to a series of somatic current steps.
source: Specifically, mPFC neurons in WIN-exposed rats showed impaired membrane reaction profiles in response to a series of somatic current steps (Figure 6A and E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A and E

claim: The resting potential was similar independent of the sex and treatment.
source: Independent of the sex and treatment, the resting potential was similar (Figure 6B and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B and F

claim: The rheobase was decreased in males prenatally exposed to WIN.
source: While the rheobase (Figure 6C and G) was decreased in males prenatally exposed to WIN, females were spared.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Females were spared from rheobase changes after prenatal WIN exposure.
source: While the rheobase (Figure 6C and G) was decreased in males prenatally exposed to WIN, females were spared.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Hyper-excitability in exposed-males was accompanied by an increased number of action potentials in response to somatic currents steps.
source: Moreover, this hyper-excitability in exposed-males was accompanied by an increased number of action potentials in response to somatic currents steps (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Similar results have been obtained in the rat progeny of dams treated with THC during gestation.
source: Similar results have been obtained in the rat progeny of dams treated with THC during gestation (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7

claim: PCE leads to an increased excitability of deep layers mPFC pyramidal cells in male progeny only.
source: Thus, PCE leads to an increased excitability of deep layers mPFC pyramidal cells in male progeny only.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figures 6 and 7

claim: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased TRPV1 mRNA in female offspring.
source: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased TRPV1, mGlu5, and DAGLα mRNA in female offspring.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8

claim: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased mGlu5 mRNA in female offspring.
source: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased TRPV1, mGlu5, and DAGLα mRNA in female offspring.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8

claim: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased DAGLα mRNA in female offspring.
source: Treatment of dams with WIN from GD5 to GD20 decreased TRPV1, mGlu5, and DAGLα mRNA in female offspring.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8

claim: The same WIN treatment decreased only mGlu5 in male offspring.
source: However, the same treatment decreased only mGlu5 in male offspring.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8

claim: CDPPB fully restored the ability of excitatory mPFC synapses to express LTD in the prenatally WIN-exposed male group.
source: We found that CDPPB fully restored the ability of excitatory mPFC synapses to express LTD in the prenatally WIN-exposed male group (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9A-B

claim: Preincubation with SR141716A prevented the CDPPB rescue of synaptic plasticity.
source: Interestingly, preincubation with either SR141716A or capsazepine prevented the CDPPB rescue of synaptic plasticity (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9C-D

claim: Preincubation with capsazepine prevented the CDPPB rescue of synaptic plasticity.
source: Interestingly, preincubation with either SR141716A or capsazepine prevented the CDPPB rescue of synaptic plasticity (Figure 9C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 9C-D

claim: Both CB1R and TRPV1 receptors are engaged in the presence of the mGlu5 PAM.
source: Thus, the data showed that both receptors are engaged in the presence of the mGlu5 PAM.
evidence: Inferred from the antagonist experiments shown in Figure 9C-D

claim: Systemic CDPPB normalized social cognition in the PCE group but remained without effect in the SHAM group.
source: Strikingly, we found that systemic CDPPB normalized social cognition in the PCE group but remained without effect in the SHAM group, indicating selectivity of the drug's effects to the disease-state (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9E-F

claim: Pre-treatment with SR141716A prevented the ameliorative actions of CDPPB on social interaction.
source: In agreement with the synaptic plasticity experiments, pre-treatment with either SR141716A (Figure 9G–H) or capsazepine prevented the ameliorative actions of CDPPB (Figure 9G–H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9G-H

claim: Pre-treatment with capsazepine prevented the ameliorative actions of CDPPB on social interaction.
source: In agreement with the synaptic plasticity experiments, pre-treatment with either SR141716A (Figure 9G–H) or capsazepine prevented the ameliorative actions of CDPPB (Figure 9G–H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 9G-H

claim: Potentiating mGlu5 signaling normalized synaptic and behavioral deficits induced by prenatal exposure to cannabinoids via CB1R and TRPV1 activation.
source: Thus, potentiating mGlu5 signaling normalized synaptic and behavioral deficits induced by prenatal exposure to cannabinoids via CB1R and TRPV1 activation.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 9

claim: Incubation of mPFC slices prepared from PCE male rats with the FAAH inhibitor URB597 effectively restored eCB-LTD.
source: Indeed, incubation of mPFC slices prepared from PCE male rats with the FAAH inhibitor URB597 effectively restored eCB-LTD (Figure 12A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 12A-B

claim: Pre-incubation with capsazepine did not prevent the curative effect of URB597 on LTD.
source: Interestingly, we found that pre-incubation with the specific TRPV1 antagonist capsazepine did not prevent the curative effect of URB597.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 12C-D

claim: The CB1R antagonist SR141716 blocked the URB597 rescue of LTD.
source: Rather, the CB1R antagonist SR141716 blocked the URB597 rescue (Figure 12C–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 12C-D

claim: In vivo treatment with the FAAH inhibitor (URB597, 0.1 mg/kg) normalized social deficits in adult male PCE rats.
source: We found that in vivo treatment with the FAAH inhibitor (URB597, 0.1 mg/kg) normalized social deficits in adult male PCE rats (Figure 12E–F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 12E-F

claim: SR141716A but not capsazepine prevented the curative actions of URB597 on social behavior.
source: In line with our mPFC slice results, SR141716A but not capsazepine prevented the curative actions of URB597 (Figure 12G–H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 12G-H

claim: Blocking anandamide degradation normalized social deficits via CB1R.
source: Thus, blocking anandamide degradation normalized social deficits via CB1R.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 12

claim: Fetal exposure to cannabinoids causes sex-specific alterations of behavioral and synaptic functions in the adult progeny.
source: We discovered that fetal exposure to cannabinoids causes sex-specific alterations of behavioral and synaptic functions in the adult progeny.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: PCE reduces social interactions in males but not females.
source: Specifically, we found that prenatal cannabinoid exposure (PCE) reduces social interactions in males but not females, while other behaviors were spared.
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings

claim: PCE specifically altered neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity in the prefrontal cortex of male rats.
source: In parallel, PCE specifically altered neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity in the prefrontal cortex of male rats.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological findings

claim: In PCE females, LTD was fully expressed in the presence of a specific CB1R antagonist (SR141716A 5 μM).
source: In PCE females, LTD was fully expressed in the presence of a specific CB1R antagonist (SR141716A 5 μM, Figure 10A–B–C) but completely prevented by TRPV1R antagonists (capsazepine 10 µM, Figure 10A–B–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10A-B-C

claim: In PCE females, LTD was completely prevented by TRPV1R antagonists (capsazepine 10 µM).
source: In PCE females, LTD was fully expressed in the presence of a specific CB1R antagonist (SR141716A 5 μM, Figure 10A–B–C) but completely prevented by TRPV1R antagonists (capsazepine 10 µM, Figure 10A–B–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 10A-B-C

claim: TRPV1R rather than CB1R mediates LTD in female PCE.
source: Thus, TRPV1R rather than CB1R mediates LTD in female PCE.
evidence: Conclusion from antagonist experiments shown in Figure 10

claim: The CB1R antagonist prevented LTD induction in rat male slices.
source: As expected from over a decade of studies in male rodents (Bender et al., 2006; Chevaleyre et al., 2006; Gerdeman et al., 2002; Iremonger et al., 2011; Lafourcade et al., 2007; Marsicano et al., 2002; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Puente et al., 2011; Robbe et al., 2002a) the CB1R antagonist prevented LTD induction in rat male slices (Figure 11D,E,F and Figure 11— figure supplement 1)).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 11D,E,F and Figure 11—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous literature

claim: CB1R antagonist treatment was without effect on LTD in female slices.
source: Unexpectedly (Rubino et al., 2015), the same treatment was without effect in female slices (Figure 11A–B–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 11A-B-C

claim: Antagonism of TRPV1R was without effect on LTD in males.
source: In contrast, antagonism of TRPV1R was without effect in males (Figure 11A–C) but prevented the induction of eCB-LTD in females (Figure 11D–E–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 11A-C

claim: Antagonism of TRPV1R prevented the induction of eCB-LTD in females.
source: In contrast, antagonism of TRPV1R was without effect in males (Figure 11A–C) but prevented the induction of eCB-LTD in females (Figure 11D–E–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 11D-E-F

claim: The doses of WIN and THC used correspond to a moderate exposure of cannabis in humans, correcting for the differences in route of administration and body weight surface area.
source: This protocol of PCE is clinically relevant, since the doses of WIN and THC used here correspond to a moderate exposure of cannabis in humans, correcting for the differences in route of administration and body weight surface area (Garcia et al., 1998; Mereu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garcia et al., 1998 and Mereu et al., 2003

claim: Basal levels of anandamide are reduced in limbic areas of prenatally WIN-exposed rats.
source: In support of this idea, basal levels of anandamide are reduced in limbic areas of prenatally WIN-exposed rats (Castelli et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castelli et al., 2007

claim: CB1R affinity is higher in males while receptor density is similar in both sexes in the limbic forebrain.
source: CB1R affinity is higher in males while receptor density is similar in both sexes in the limbic forebrain; however, in the mesencephalon both parameters are higher in males (Rodríguez de Fonseca et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodríguez de Fonseca et al., 1994

claim: In the mesencephalon, both CB1R affinity and receptor density are higher in males.
source: CB1R affinity is higher in males while receptor density is similar in both sexes in the limbic forebrain; however, in the mesencephalon both parameters are higher in males (Rodríguez de Fonseca et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodríguez de Fonseca et al., 1994

claim: In the PFC, CB1R density is lower in males than in females.
source: In the PFC, CB1R density is lower in males than in females (Castelli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castelli et al., 2014

claim: Female prelimbic cortex pyramidal neurons have smaller/less complex apical dendritic arbors than in males.
source: At the structural level, the medial PFC of rats is also sexually different: female prelimbic cortex pyramidal neurons have smaller/less complex apical dendritic arbors than in males (Garrett and Wellman, 2009; Kolb and Stewart, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garrett and Wellman, 2009 and Kolb and Stewart, 1991

claim: Sexual differences in fear-conditioning have been identified.
source: At the behavioral level, sexual differences in fear-conditioning have also been identified (Gruene et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2001; Pryce et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gruene et al., 2015; Gupta et al., 2001; Pryce et al., 1999

claim: Active avoidance displays sex differences.
source: For instance, active avoidance (Dalla and Shors, 2009), spatial memory (Dalla and Shors, 2009; Qi et al., 2016) and hippocampal LTP (Gupta et al., 2001; Maren, 1995; Qi et al., 2016) display sex differences.
